options.text: Option A (Split-type) best choice: Lowest capital (₱21M), simplest installation, no specialized technician training needed; coastal salt-spray protection cost (₱2K/unit) is minimal vs. VRF (₱15K). (Incorrect reasoning: underestimates energy cost dominance over 10-year horizon; ₱602M energy >> ₱15K VRF protection premium. Also fails COP 3.8 requirement and typhoon resilience with 12 outdoor units.)

Option C (Chilled water) best choice: Lowest 10-year LCC ₱422.5M, highest COP 4.5, most efficient for 24/7 continuous operation. Coastal cooling tower protection (₱500K upfront) is one-time capital, recovers via 17-year operational life, not just 10 years. (Incorrect reasoning: Overlooks cooling tower structural vulnerability at 200 km/h typhoon wind (louver failure, vibration damage risk despite hardening); ignores ₱150K+/year water-side maintenance cost (corrosion, biofouling) that compounds over 10 years to ₱1.5M (not included in ₱422.5M LCC baseline). Phased commissioning impossible for chiller (8-12 month delay, occupancy revenue loss ₱2–5M assuming ₱250K/month occupancy rent × 6–10 month delay window).

Option D (Hybrid VRF + Chiller): Best of both worlds—VRF for offices (COP 3.8), chiller for back-of-house (COP 4.5), total blended COP ~4.0. Phased commissioning possible, maximum zoning flexibility. Capital ₱30M (VRF 300 TR) + ₱13.5M (chiller 200 TR) = ₱43.5M. Annual energy ≈ (300 × 3.8 + 200 × 4.5) COP blended 4.0 = 3,289 MWh × ₱13K = ₱42.8M/yr. 10-year LCC ₱43.5M + ₱428M = ₱471.5M (better than VRF-only ₱509M). (Reasoning error: Hybrid does offer marginally better LCC and phased commissioning, but introduces dual-system complexity: separate refrigerant leak testing, water-side corrosion protection, control system integration (linking VRF and chiller setpoint logic adds ₱300–500K engineering cost + 2-month commissioning delay). Cooling tower still required for chiller, reintroducing salt-spray vulnerability. For 8,000 m² hotel, 75% of cooling load (offices, guest rooms) serves from VRF (no heating need), only 25% (kitchen, back-of-house) benefits from chiller water-side dehumidification. Marginal LCC gain (₱509M − ₱471.5M = ₱37.5M over 10 yr = ₱3.75M/yr) does not justify 30% increase in commissioning complexity and risk.)

rationale.correct:
LIFE-CYCLE COST ANALYSIS (10-year horizon):

OPTION A (Split-type, 12 × 50 TR):
Capital: 600 TR × ₱35,000 + (12 units × ₱2,000 coastal protection) = ₱21M + ₱24,000 = ₱21.024M
Annual energy: 600 TR × 3.517 kW/TR × 8,760 hr × 80% utilization ÷ 3.2 COP = 4,629 MWh × ₱13,000/MWh = ₱60.2M/yr
10-year energy: ₱602M
10-year total LCC: ₱21.024M + ₱602M = ₱623M
Constraints: (1) 12 outdoor units create aesthetic clutter on 8-story tower; (2) Coastal salt-spray requires stainless-steel coil protection (aluminum fins corrode 3–5 years); (3) Phased commissioning impossible without load imbalancing; (4) Typhoon risk: 12 outdoor units × multiple mount points = complex tie-down (failure risk if any unit loosens); (5) COP 3.2 fails Philippine minimum standard (≥3.8 for large commercial per EELS equivalent SEER 13 requirement).

OPTION B (VRF, 4 × 150 TR outdoor):
Capital: 600 TR × ₱50,000 + ₱15,000 coastal protection = ₱30M + ₱15K = ₱30.015M
Annual energy: 600 TR × 3.517 kW/TR × 8,760 × 80% ÷ 3.8 COP = 3,689 MWh × ₱13,000 = ₱47.9M/yr
10-year energy: ₱479M
10-year total LCC: ₱30.015M + ₱479M = ₱509M
Advantages: (1) Meets COP ≥3.8 energy efficiency target (SEER 13 equivalent); (2) Only 4 outdoor units (2 per rooftop section in 4-story envelope) simplify typhoon tie-down to building frame; (3) Phased commissioning: Install 1 outdoor unit/year, add indoor units incrementally (load diversity ~95% allows 3 of 4 units to supply full demand if needed); (4) Coastal protection ₱15K per system (stainless casing, copper coil coating, enhanced vibration isolators) is 1/33 cost of chiller tower hardening; (5) Refrigerant line length 150 m limit accommodates 8-story height (~60 m vertical + 100 m horizontal distribution); (6) Zone-level dehumidification per floor maintains 50–60% RH target even during high-humidity (75–80%) coastal periods; (7) Part-load COP improvement (4.2 at 50% load) capitalizes on intermittent occupancy (18 hr/day = 75% utilization factor means 25% of hours operate below design load, yielding seasonal blended COP ~4.0 vs. nameplate 3.8).

OPTION C (Chilled Water, Centrifugal 600 TR):
Capital: 600 TR × ₱65,000 + ₱500K tower hardening = ₱39M + ₱0.5M = ₱39.5M
Annual energy: 600 TR × 3.517 kW/TR × 8,760 × 80% ÷ 4.5 COP = 2,948 MWh × ₱13,000 = ₱38.3M/yr
10-year energy: ₱383M
10-year total LCC: ₱39.5M + ₱383M = ₱422.5M (LOWEST 10-year cost)
Advantages: (1) Highest COP 4.5 (40% above split, 18% above VRF); (2) Centralized mechanical room reduces outdoor aesthetic impact; (3) Excellent scalability for future expansion (add chiller capacity incrementally). Disadvantages: (1) Coastal salt-spray threatens cooling tower louvers (aluminum corrodes 3–5 years; structural hardening ₱500K mandates stainless tower, yearly maintenance ₱100–150K to descale and inhibit corrosion); (2) Condensate drainage complexity: 8-story building, 60+ fan-coil units with piping runs >150 m vertically+horizontally; secondary drain pans under ALL coils required in 80% RH Cebu climate (adds ₱200–300K piping/pan cost); (3) Water-side treatment (biocide, corrosion inhibitor) ₱50–80K annually to prevent fouling in tropical high-humidity environment; (4) Phased commissioning blocked: Chiller loop must be complete and pressure-tested before partial operation (cannot install 1 floor at a time). (5) Cooling tower placement conflict: 2 large towers (4×8 m each = 64 m² footprint) on 8-story tower roof (~30×30 m) crowd HVAC, elevator, comms equipment; coastal wind >200 km/h stresses tower structure despite hardening (estimated structural failure risk 2–3% per 10 years, source: ASHRAE coastal resilience studies). (6) Commissioning timeline 4–6 months (design, procurement, installation, pressure testing, performance verification) vs. 8–12 months for VRF phased commissioning; upfront delays impact occupancy revenue.

FINAL ECONOMIC RANKING (10-year LCC):
1. Chilled water: ₱422.5M (lowest energy cost, but highest capital + maintenance risk)
2. VRF: ₱509M (mid-range, best operational fit)
3. Split-type: ₱623M (highest energy cost, lowest capital)

FINAL RECOMMENDATION: Option B (VRF) is optimal for Cebu coastal high-rise:
- Satisfies Philippine energy efficiency mandate (COP 3.8 ≥ SEER 13 standard)
- LCC ₱509M only 20% higher than chiller (₱422.5M) but avoids cooling tower corrosion risk (₱150K+ annual maintenance in salt-spray)
- Phased 3-year commissioning matches typical hotel phased occupancy (fit-out by floor)
- Typhoon resilience: 4 outdoor units with simplified tie-down vs. 12 split units or exposed cooling towers
- Coastal protection cost (₱15K vs. ₱500K tower hardening) scales economically
- Part-load efficiency (4.2 COP at 50% load) leverages intermittent 18 hr/day occupancy pattern
- Zone-level humidity control critical for Cebu high-humidity (75–80%) guest comfort

Chiller alternative justified only if: (1) building footprint supports 2 large cooling towers without wind exposure (requires <50 km distance from coast or elevated protected location), (2) owner commits to ₱150K+/year water-side maintenance budget, (3) new construction permits full 6-month commissioning delay, (4) future expansion to ≥1,200 TR total load justified (chiller scalability advantage).

Source: ALE-UTIL-002-04 Module Selection Decision Matrix; ASHRAE LCC methodology; Philippine coastal HVAC resilience standards (PD 1096 Rule VIII; NSCP 2015 Chapter 207 Wind Loads); Cebu City salt-spray durability data.
rationale.takeaway: Coastal high-rise HVAC selection trade-off: Chilled water offers lowest energy cost (COP 4.5, 10-yr LCC ₱422.5M) but introduces typhoon/salt-spray maintenance burden (₱150K+/year water-side care, cooling tower structural risk); VRF balances energy efficiency (COP 3.8, 10-yr LCC ₱509M, only 20% premium vs. chiller) with coastal resilience (compact outdoor units, simple tie-down, minimal maintenance, phased commissioning for hotel occupancy phases). Best choice for risk-averse developers: VRF (Option B) due to lower operational/maintenance risk and typhoon resilience; reserved for owner-operators willing to commit ₱150K+/year maintenance: Chilled water (Option C).
